units: the metalworker describes his place of labour as a living creature
he gives the device that sends air the role of a lung
he explains that without that air the burning weakens
he likens the block he strikes on to a shoulder
he presents the gripping tools as fearless fingers
he says those tools take hold of the burning metal without faltering
he compares the hearth itself to an organ that beats
his pupil asks him which part she stands for in this anatomy
he answers that she will be the memory of the movements
text: The blacksmith spoke about his workshop as though it were some drowsing animal, and he named its limbs for her patiently, one after another. The bellows, he said, performed the office of a lung: starve the coals of that slow, deliberate breath and the burning slackens, the bar surrenders its heat. The anvil, meanwhile, served as a shoulder, absorbing the entire violence of the hammer without ever flinching. The tongs, he insisted, were fingers considerably braver than his own, since they closed upon glowing metal and never once trembled. As for the hearth, he likened it to a heart beating dully at the further end of the room. His apprentice listened without interrupting, then asked him which limb she herself stood for in this anatomy. She would be the memory, he answered, the keeper of every movement once the old man's hands had surrendered.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: weaving began as an entirely manual operation
the earliest devices held the threads upright
lumps of clay served to keep those threads taut
the worker put the crosswise thread in row by row
a device worked by foot then parted the threads to open a passage
the tool carrying the crosswise thread crossed the width in one movement
a cord and a mallet then threw that tool mechanically
the output doubled without calling for a second worker
punched cards later governed the lifting of each thread
the pattern moved from human memory to a coded support
text: Weaving lived in the fingers long before it belonged to any machinery. The earliest frames held their threads upright, weighted at the foot by lumps of baked clay, while the worker carried the crosswise thread through by hand, one patient row after another. Then arrived the frame governed by the feet: pedals lifted a whole company of threads and opened a clean passage, so the carrier crossed the entire width in a single throw. Afterwards that carrier was thrown mechanically, flung by a cord and a mallet, which doubled the output without demanding a second worker. Later still, punched cards commanded the lifting of every individual thread, and the pattern migrated out of a weaver's memory onto a coded support. Each stage removed a movement of the hand. None removed the eye that watches the tension.

units: the glassy layer is not a paint laid on the surface
the heat turns a mineral deposit into glass
the maker spreads a preparation of powders before the firing
those powders melt and then spread into one unbroken layer
the cooling sets the material without any crystal structure
that absence of crystals explains the clearness obtained
the sealing of the pores stops the liquid from seeping through
the hardness of the layer protects the wall from scratches
an uneven shrinking between the two materials brings a web of fine cracks
text: A glaze is not a coat of paint laid over the surface of a pot. It is glass, and the heat manufactures it on the clay itself. The potter coats the piece in a slurry of finely ground minerals, then surrenders it to the kiln. Under the firing those powders melt and spread into one unbroken layer; as they cool they harden without becoming crystalline again, and that is precisely where their clearness originates. Because the layer seals the pores of the wall, the vessel stops weeping and becomes fit to hold a liquid. Because the layer is hard, it equally protects the surface against every kind of scratch. An imbalance between the two materials produces a familiar defect: should the glass contract more than the clay while cooling, it splits into a web of exceedingly fine cracks.

units: a storage cupboard arrives in the workshop out of shape
its doors no longer close properly
the joiner fears that taking it apart will break the old joints
damping the panel fails because the curve returns on drying
planing the rebate makes the door gape on the opposite side
the craftsman notices that the twisting does not affect the whole height
he finds that a split rail is turning the side panel
he puts a sound rail in place of the cracked piece
he holds the joint under pressure until the glue has set
the cupboard stands true again and its doors work
text: The cupboard delivered to the workshop was standing by luck alone: one side panel had twisted and the doors no longer closed properly. The joiner hesitated to dismantle the whole thing, since the ancient joints would probably burst under the pressure. He first attempted damping the panel to persuade it straight, but the timber curled back the moment it dried. Then he planed the rebate, and discovered that the door simply gaped along the opposite edge. The answer emerged from patient observation: the side was not bowed over its whole height, it was pivoting on a single split rail. He replaced the cracked rail with a sound one, held the joint in a clamp until the glue had thoroughly set, and hung the hinges again. The panel recovered its uprightness, and both doors swung sweetly once more.

units: the text compares two ways of finishing the edge of a cloth
the hand method consists of turning the edge over twice
the iron serves to press each fold before the stitching
the hand stitches catch only one thread on the visible side
the hand finish calls for patience and moves along without haste
the stitching done by hand becomes invisible on the right side
the machine method takes up the same double fold
closely set pins hold the cloth before it goes under the needle
the machine finish stands up better to repeated washing
the machine stitching leaves a visible line on the outer face
text: Want a hem that hangs perfectly straight, with no ripples and no lumps? Weigh up the two ways of building it before you put a single stitch in. By hand, you turn the edge over, press it flat, turn it again, and work a blind stitch that catches barely a thread on the visible side. It takes an age, it demands patience and a thoroughly steady temper, but the stitching disappears completely and the cloth keeps all its softness. On the machine, you prepare exactly the same double fold, pin it closely, and run an even line along the edge of the foot. It is quick, it is strong, and it survives repeated washing far better than handwork; the trade is a line showing distinctly on the outer face. So ask yourself which matters more: that it lasts for seasons, or that nobody ever notices it.

units: a charity teaches the metal trades to adults changing career
the classes are held under the roof beams of an old market hall
the workshops are grouped by family of movement
the first workshop teaches how to lay an even bead without burning through the sheet
the second deals with assembly by pieces put in cold
the third covers the finishing treatment obtained by heating and oiling
the last workshop teaches the costing of a commission and the buying of stock
the woman in charge states that people rarely drop out over the craft
the paperwork often wears the trainees down
text: Under the roof beams of an old market hall, a charity teaches the metal trades to adults changing career, and its workshops are grouped by family of movement. The first is given over to welding, where pupils learn to lay an even bead without burning through the sheet. The second covers mechanical assembly, in which every rivet must be driven cold, into a hole bored carefully to size. The third handles finishing, and a good deal of discussion goes into the patina you draw out by heating the piece and afterwards oiling it. The final workshop is the unexpected one, and it concerns costing: pricing a commission, buying materials, promising a date you can honour. Few people withdraw over the craft itself, the woman in charge explains; the paperwork is what wears them down. A fresh group begins at the end of the season.

units: the dye workshop smells of wet ash from first light
boards cover the vats that are still cold
the water in the troughs keeps the colour of the day before
the dyer lights a fire under the widest vat
she draws a mass of undyed yarn out of a basket
steam rises and the bath takes on the shade of crushed leaves
the wool put under takes up the colour very quickly
the next stage consists of rinsing the yarn in one trough after another
the yarn hung under the lean-to drips and marks the ground
text: At first light the dye house smells of wet ash and sodden wool. The vats are still sleeping beneath their thick wooden boards, and the water inside them retains the darkened colour of the previous day. Soon the dyer kindles a fire beneath the widest of them, then lifts a skein of undyed yarn out of a basket and shakes it vigorously at arm's length to loosen the knots. Steam begins to rise, the bath turns the shade of crushed leaves, and the wool descends into it all at once, without hesitating, drinking the colour in like a sponge. The rinsing follows: the skeins travel from one trough to the next, paler each time, heavier between the fingers. By evening they hang in a close row beneath the lean-to, still streaming, each one leaving on the ground a stain of the shade it has taken.

units: the writer disputes the idea that the electronic tool makes the older method pointless
the optical device gives a vertical from its own footing
a sinking of that footing falsifies the measurement with no visible warning
the hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts
the apprentice who handles this instrument grasps in the body what he is checking
newer teams no longer question what the screen displays
they do not check a measurement by a second method
costly reworking follows from this on site
the firm puts that reworking down to a lack of attention
the writer holds that passing on the older skill is not nostalgia
text: To claim that the electronic instrument makes learning the plumb line pointless is a failure of reasoning, and the failure costs money on site. An optical device delivers a vertical immediately, but it delivers it from its own footing; let the tripod settle or the ground shudder, and the error propagates with nothing whatever to announce it. The hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts, and the apprentice who has handled it understands physically what he is checking. Lacking that understanding, newer teams no longer think to doubt the screen, nor to confirm a value by a second method. Expensive reworking follows, and the company attributes it to carelessness when it truly comes from a truncated training. Passing on the older skill is therefore no exercise in nostalgia.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the instrument maker has taken over from her old master
the custom of the workshop was thinning at the time of the handover
amateur players wanted an instrument that held its tune
those players could not afford a piece shaped entirely by hand
she refused to use a timber of poorer quality
she split the making into two separate sets
the parts with no bearing on the sound are made in batches by a workshop nearby
she shapes alone the pieces that settle the sound
the price fell by a third with no loss of tone
her old master recognised her hand on hearing the instrument
text: The instrument maker described here took over her old master's workshop at precisely the moment when its custom was thinning. She quickly identified an obstacle which no catalogue resolved: amateur players wanted an instrument that held its tune, without being able to afford a piece cut entirely by hand. Rather than descend to a timber of poorer quality, she divided her work into two separate sets. The parts with no bearing whatever on the sound, the rough neck and the ribs, now arrive in batches from a workshop nearby. The parts that settle the sound, the belly and the bass bar, she shapes alone and adjusts them by ear. The price fell by a third, the tone lost nothing at all, and her old master, who arrived to hear a finished commission, recognised his own hand in the varnish.

units: two ranges of chairs are shown in the same room
the first range comes from a workshop attached to the old joints
that range uses fitted tenons and a back bent under steam
its sturdiness commands the respect of the writer of the review
its drawing seems hesitant for want of attention paid to the outline
the second range comes from a studio using machine cutting
this second range is made in plywood
its seat meets the back with no cushion added
the object comes apart in a handful of movements
the reviewer judges that neither range clearly wins
text: Two ranges of chairs occupy the same exhibition room, and the pairing teaches you something. The first emerges from a workshop that makes a point of traditional jointing: tenons pared to fit, a back bent under steam, an oiled finish. Its sturdiness commands respect, yet the drawing hesitates, as though the maker had spent all his attention upon structure and neglected the outline. The second comes from a studio that cheerfully owns up to machine cutting and plywood. Its line is clean, the seat meets the back without any cushion added, and the whole object comes apart in a handful of movements. One regrets, however, the dryness of the edges, which no passing hand will ever soften. Neither range clearly triumphs: one will outlast its owner, the other will please the eye before tiring at the joints.
